q270: Wrote down her inner critic's words and answered them as she would answer a friend
q271: Set a good-enough standard and a time limit for each drawing before starting
q272: Practised a self-compassion break after every mistake
q273: Shared one draft early with her team each week, on purpose before it was perfect
q274: Listed her values to remember why she loved design
q275: Paul writes, whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord (Colossians 3:23). Heartily means with love and full effort, not with fear. God accepts us in Christ before we perform (Ephesians 1:6). Jesus said His yoke is easy and His burden is light (Matthew 11:30), which is very different from the crushing weight of having to be perfect. Even Paul admitted he had not already attained, but kept pressing forward (Philippians 3:12). Growth is the goal, not flawlessness. Ananya could now work as a beloved daughter offering her gifts, not as an employee trying to earn her place in the family of God.
q276: God designed us to learn through mistakes. Research suggests the brain shows a special signal when we notice an error, and this is how learning happens. A person who is terrified of mistakes often learns more slowly, because fear narrows thinking and creativity. Self-compassion, in studies, is linked with more motivation to improve, not less. When we treat ourselves kindly, the brain's threat system calms down and the parts used for problem-solving and creativity work better. We were made to grow like a plant, little by little, not to appear finished from the start.
q277: Psalm 103:14|For he knoweth our frame, he remembereth that we are dust.
q281: Ananya now finishes most work on time. She still feels the pull to redraw, and once she stayed late again before a big client meeting. But mistakes no longer cost her three nights of sleep. Her team lead noticed she was sharing ideas more freely. She has started sketching for fun again on weekends, just for the joy of it.
q282: Excellence flows from love and rest, while perfectionism flows from fear and never lets us finish.
q283: You do not have to be perfect for God to love you. Doing your best and learning from mistakes is enough.
q284: Priya and the word she could not say
q285: Priya, 26, HR executive in Delhi, active youth volunteer at her church
q286: Priya said yes to everything. She ran the church Sunday school, edited the youth newsletter, sang in the choir and helped her aunt with her catering business every Saturday. At work she covered for colleagues who went home early. When her cousin asked to borrow money for the third time, she gave it, though she had not been repaid before. She was always smiling, and everybody said she was so helpful. But inside she was furious and tired. She cried in the bathroom at the office and felt guilty for feeling resentful. When she tried to say no to her pastor about leading another event, her throat closed up and she heard herself say, Of course, happy to help.
q287: People-pleasing often grows from a childhood where love felt conditional, where being good and useful kept the peace. Priya was the eldest daughter in a home with a stressed father, and she learned early that keeping everyone happy kept things calm. Her nervous system treated someone's disappointment as a threat, and her body chose the fawn response: appease, agree, smooth things over. Each yes brought short relief and avoided conflict, which reinforced the habit. Underneath was a belief that her worth depended on being needed and that saying no was selfish and unchristian.
q288: Her small group leader asked a simple question: When you say yes to everyone, who are you saying no to? Priya thought for a while and answered, Myself, my rest, and maybe God. That week she wrote her first boundary script.
q289: Paused before answering any request, saying let me check and get back to you
q290: Used DEAR MAN to tell her pastor she would step back from one ministry
q291: Wrote short boundary scripts and practised them aloud in the mirror
q292: Told her cousin kindly that she could not lend more money
q293: Did a HALT check when she felt resentful, noticing if she was tired or hungry
q294: Jesus did not say yes to everyone. When crowds were looking for Him, He went to other towns (Mark 1:35-38). He often withdrew to pray (Luke 5:16). His yes and no came from listening to His Father, not from fear of people. Paul asks, do I seek to please men? If I yet pleased men, I should not be the servant of Christ (Galatians 1:10). Jesus taught, let your yea be yea, and your nay, nay (Matthew 5:37). A loving no is honest. Priya learned that serving out of fear and resentment is not the same as serving out of love, and that God's love for her did not depend on how useful she was.
q295: God made us to belong, so the brain is very sensitive to social rejection. Research suggests that social pain activates some of the same brain areas as physical pain, which is why saying no can feel so scary. But God also gave us the ability to grow new patterns. Every time Priya said a kind, clear no and nothing terrible happened, her brain gathered new evidence that relationships can survive boundaries. Rest and limits protect the body from chronic stress. Healthy boundaries actually make real love possible, because we give freely rather than under pressure.
q296: Galatians 1:10|For do I now persuade men, or God? or do I seek to please men?
q300: It was hard. Her aunt was upset for a month, and one choir member stopped speaking to her for a while. Priya felt guilty many times and sometimes slipped back into an automatic yes. But she has more energy now, and the bathroom crying stopped. She still serves, but now with a cheerful heart, and her friendships feel more honest.
q301: A loving no makes room for a wholehearted yes to God.
q302: It is okay to say no sometimes. Jesus said no too, and saying no kindly helps us say yes with a happy heart.
q303: Daniel and the walk to the church door
q304: Daniel, 19, engineering student in Shillong, Meghalaya, from a Khasi Christian family
q305: Daniel loved God, but Sunday mornings filled him with dread. Walking into church meant greeting aunties, shaking hands with elders and being asked about his studies. His face would burn red, his voice would shake and he was sure everyone could see how awkward he was. He started arriving late and sitting in the last row, then leaving during the final hymn before anyone could talk to him. When the youth leader asked him to read Scripture aloud, he made an excuse and did not come the next week. His parents thought he was losing his faith. Inside, Daniel felt lonely and ashamed, wishing he could be like the confident boys in the youth group who seemed so at ease.
q306: Social anxiety is an intense fear of being judged or embarrassed. Daniel's brain had become very good at scanning for signs of disapproval and overestimating how much others noticed him. Research suggests socially anxious people often focus attention inwards on their own blushing and shaking, which makes the feelings stronger. Avoiding church conversations brought quick relief, but it taught his brain that people were dangerous and that he could not cope. As a shy child he had been laughed at in school for his stammer, and that memory still shaped how he expected people to react.
q307: A visiting counsellor at a youth camp explained that most people are far too busy thinking about themselves to notice our blushing. Daniel laughed for the first time about his fear. He decided to try small experiments rather than wait for the fear to disappear on its own.
q308: Made a fear ladder starting with arriving five minutes early and sitting one row further forward
q309: Used the physiological sigh in the car park before walking in
q310: Named his feelings silently, saying this is fear of judgment, not truth
q311: Shifted attention outward by asking others simple questions
q312: Asked one kind elder to be a friendly face each week
q313: Read a short Scripture passage to just three friends before reading in church
q314: Moses told God he was slow of speech, and God did not reject him. He said, I will be with thy mouth (Exodus 4:10-12). Timothy was timid, and Paul encouraged him that God gives power, love and a sound mind (2 Timothy 1:7). The fear of man bringeth a snare, but whoso putteth his trust in the LORD shall be safe (Proverbs 29:25). Daniel learned that his belonging in God's family did not depend on being smooth or confident. The church is a body where every part matters, including the shy ones (1 Corinthians 12:22). He was already accepted in Christ, so he did not need to earn acceptance from every person in the pew.
q315: God designed the brain to adapt to what we practise. When we gently approach the situations we fear, the alarm system slowly learns they are safe. In studies, graded exposure is one of the most helpful approaches for social anxiety. Turning attention outward to other people reduces the inward focus that feeds the fear. God also wired us for belonging, and safe faces calm the nervous system. A friendly elder's smile can help a young person's body settle. Each small step is like walking a new path through a field until it becomes an easy road.
q316: Proverbs 29:25|The fear of man bringeth a snare: but whoso putteth his trust in the LORD shall be safe.
q320: After four months Daniel stayed for tea after the service most weeks. He still blushes and his voice still shakes a little when he reads, but he read a full psalm aloud in the youth service. Some Sundays the dread came back, especially after exams, and he skipped once. But he kept climbing his ladder, and now he helps welcome new students.
q321: Courage is not the absence of blushing but taking the next small step while trusting God.
q322: Feeling shy is okay. Taking little brave steps, with God and a kind friend, helps the scared feeling get smaller.
q323: Meera and the mind that would not switch off
q324: Meera, 47, school teacher in Kolkata, married, caring for her elderly mother-in-law
q325: By day Meera was busy with forty students, lesson plans and her mother-in-law's medicines. But the moment she lay down at night, her mind switched on like a television. Did she submit the exam marks? Was her mother-in-law's cough getting worse? What did the principal mean by that comment? She lay awake for two or three hours, scrolling her phone to distract herself, then checking the time and panicking about how little sleep she would get. She dragged herself through the next day on strong tea, irritable and foggy. She tried praying, but her prayers turned into worry lists. After six months she began to dread bedtime itself.
q326: During a busy day, the mind has no space to process what is happening. When things finally go quiet at night, the brain's default mode network, a system that wanders and reviews, starts replaying the day. Stress hormones that should drop in the evening stay high. Bright phone screens can delay the body's natural sleep hormone, melatonin. Over time the brain links the bed with being awake and anxious, so lying down itself becomes a trigger. Clock-watching adds pressure, and trying hard to sleep makes sleep harder. Meera also believed that rest was lazy as long as anyone in the family needed something.
q327: A doctor ruled out thyroid and other medical causes and told her, Your body knows how to sleep, but your mind needs a place to put the day down. Meera realised she had never given herself any time to unwind. She decided to build a wind-down, not just collapse into bed.
q328: Did a brain dump on paper at nine each night, writing every task and worry
q329: Kept a short worry time after school so worries had a place during the day
q330: Put her phone outside the bedroom and used an old alarm clock
q331: Followed a simple wind-down routine of a warm bath, dim lights and a psalm
q332: Got up and sat in another room if awake more than twenty minutes, returning when sleepy
q333: God gives His beloved sleep (Psalm 127:2). The psalmist says, I will both lay me down in peace, and sleep: for thou, LORD, only makest me dwell in safety (Psalm 4:8). Sleep is an act of trust. It means admitting that God runs the world while we are unconscious. He who keeps Israel neither slumbers nor sleeps (Psalm 121:4), so we do not have to stay awake on guard. Jesus Himself slept in a storm. Meera began to see bedtime as handing the day back to God, including the unfinished marks and her mother-in-law's cough. Writing her worries down and then praying over the page became a small act of casting her care on Him.
q334: God designed sleep as a nightly repair shop. In studies, sleep helps the brain clear waste, store memories and reset emotions. The body runs on a daily rhythm, and dim light in the evening helps it release melatonin at the right time. Writing tasks down before bed, research suggests, can help some people fall asleep faster, because the brain stops trying to hold everything. Relaxing the muscles tells the nervous system the day is over. When we get out of bed after long wakefulness, the brain slowly relearns that bed is for sleep, not for worry.
q335: Psalm 4:8|I will both lay me down in peace, and sleep: for thou, LORD, only makest me dwell in safety.
q339: It took about six weeks before Meera noticed a change. She now falls asleep within half an hour on most nights. Exam weeks still bring restless nights, and once a family crisis gave her a week of poor sleep. But she no longer dreads bedtime. She feels less irritable and has started a short evening prayer time with her husband.
q340: Sleep comes more easily when we put the day down on paper and into God's hands.
q341: At night, write your worries down and give them to God. Then your mind can rest and you can sleep.
q342: Pastor Samuel and the empty cup
q343: Samuel, 51, pastor of a growing church in a town near Madurai, Tamil Nadu, married with three children
